questions.answer: Yes. Vienna has some student housings + a lot of shared appartement opportunities (called "WG"). These can be found on wg-gesuch website.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Vienna has a good transport system so living off campus isn't a problem. Living in the "northerm" district of Vienna should help, as they are closer from both campuses.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Courses get filled really quickly. To register to it, you need first to be registered at the uni, that can only be done in person. In other words, the earlier you arrive in Vienna, the more choices of class you have.
In reality, you can always try to mail a professor if his class is full and you really want it.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Contacting directly the professors can be game changing when a course is full. If you could not register for all classses, ask around you and for sure you'll hear feedback and get plenty of ideas for other courses you could take instead.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I arrived beginning of September so I still had some choice. For someone arriving at the end of the September, it might get more complicated to get all their courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
At BOKU, the timetable isn't organised in hours block like in KU. This means that a lot of classes partly overlap. When looking at the classes, check carefully at the class schedule, at which campus the course is (two main campus at ~30min from each other), what class type it is. Some classes can be easily missed (so overlap isn't much of a pb), but some are seminars cannot be missed (making overlap impossible). 
The course system is pretty chaotic compared to KU's. As a general rule, I'd recommend to be as flexible as possible there. Write to professors in case of overlap and trouble, they are used to students having these issues.

Additional comments:

questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Level highly depends on the course. You can always drop out a course in the first weeks in the level is not adapted and take something else instead.
Also the courses are always super small credits, so you never really get in any depth in a subject. The difficulty is not really the course itself, but having to deal with like 10 different subjects at the same time during the semester.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching is pretty much the same, though maybe less "discussion-based" and more top-down than in Denmark.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.answer: Master thesis and Master thesis seminar (depends of your institute)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
There's a ton of classes offered at BOKU, prioritize what you like most. 

If you miss some credits and lack space in your timetable: "Exploratory data analysis with R" and "Integrated flood risk management" are two good examples of courses you can easily overlap with seminars. Both could be taken with nearly no attending. Good in case you have no space left in your timetable but still need credits (good quality of online material).

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not have any unexpected costs. Be careful though, you'll need to pay by cash a lot of things, especially in bars or cheap restaurants. That's even more true when you go out of the city. So just be sure to always have a bit of cash when going out.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Any item is cheaper than in Copenhagen: housing, groceries, going out for food, drinks, cinema, museum, .....

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Students could join some cultural and sport events offered by the student union ÖH or ESN.
MUSI offers a lot sport opportunities for a cheap price. You'll be mixed with students and staff from all universities in Vienna, which is also nice to meet other people.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I'd recommend to join some of the ESN events, especially in the first weeks. It's the best way to meet some internationals that are also new to the city and that are seeking to make new friends. 
I'd also suggest joining a MUSI sport activity, to meet more local people. Speaking a bit of German could help for the sport class + it's also a great way to learn it.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
- With about 1h train towards the west, you can reach a lot of moutains and really nice hikes. If you're under 26, I'd suggest to get the "Vorteilscard Jugend" from ÖBB, the national train company, to get cheaper trains for the year.

- City-wise, Budapest and Prague are also a few hours of train from Vienna. Regiojet (a czech train company) offers attractive prices for both destination.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy. At university, you'll get to meet a lot of people ready to share about Vienna.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: As mentionned above, I'd recommend to join some sport course at MUSI, maybe one of the best way to meet new (local) people. At Uni or anywhere, you'll be able to meet a lot of locals. Speaking German is the biggest key to socialize with local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find any challenging cultural difference. The hardest part was to get used to Austrian bureaucry.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Vienna is vibrant city, at the heart of Europe, meaning it has some kind of unique mix of germanic, latin and slavic worlds blended together. People here will like to know more about you and your country. The hiking/outdoor culture is also great here (that's even more a thing for Western Asutria people, like in Tyrol):

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Be ready for the administrative work at BOKU + with the mess of class registration. However, you can't do much about it, so just try to be flexible.
- Go around and visit Austria. Time goes really fast in Erasmus.
- Most importantly, have fun!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Learning/speaking some German will make your life easier at any aspects (city administration, university administration, socialising, etc)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting so many amazing people and learning so many new things has been an incredible experience. Studying in another country is truly enriching, and I highly recommend it to everyone. It opens your mind to different perspectives, new ways of doing things, and unique approaches to problem-solving. While Austria and Denmark may not be worlds apart culturally, the differences are just enough to make the experience both eye-opening and rewarding.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: My biggest challenge was adjusting to Austrian bureaucracy, understanding how the course system works here, and figuring out how to fulfill all my credit requirements. The first few weeks were especially stressful and frustrating, as I often had to make last-minute changes, for instance because the entire schedule for a class would be changed just the day before it was supposed to start.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you’re part of a double degree program and writing your thesis at BOKU, don’t expect to finish it in just one sharp semester. While it’s theoretically possible, it seems nearly impossible in practice. Local students often take up to a year to complete theirs. Of course, the timeline depends on you and your supervisor, but I’d recommend planning for at least 6 to 7 months just for the thesis. Also, keep in mind that even after you’ve finished writing, you’ll need an extra month before your defense due to administrative procedures.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
